claim: Lesions to network hubs in the human thalamus are associated with multi-domain behavioral impairments in language, memory, and executive functions.
source: Previously (Hwang et al., 2021), we reported that lesions to network hubs in the human thalamus are associated with multi-domain behavioral impairments in language, memory, and executive functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Hwang et al., 2021).

claim: The anterior, medial, and posterior-medial thalamus exhibit hub-like activity profiles that are suggestive of broad functional participation.
source: Specifically, the anterior, medial, and posterior-medial thalamus exhibit hub-like activity profiles that are suggestive of broad functional participation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript showing task hub patterns in these thalamic regions.

claim: Thalamic task hubs overlap with network hubs interlinking cortical systems.
source: These thalamic task hubs overlapped with network hubs interlinking cortical systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing spatial correspondence between task hubs and functional connectivity hubs.

claim: Thalamic activity can be used to predict cortical task activity.
source: To further determine the cognitive relevance of thalamic activity and thalamocortical functional connectivity, we built a data-driven thalamocortical model to test whether thalamic activity can be used to predict cortical task activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the thalamocortical activity flow model results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The thalamocortical model predicted task-specific cortical activity patterns and outperformed comparison models built on cortical, hippocampal, and striatal regions.
source: The thalamocortical model predicted task-specific cortical activity patterns, and outperformed comparison models built on cortical, hippocampal, and striatal regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by data comparing the thalamocortical model to other brain region models.

claim: Simulated lesions to low-dimensional, multi-task thalamic hub regions impaired task activity prediction.
source: Simulated lesions to low-dimensional, multi-task thalamic hub regions impaired task activity prediction.
evidence: This claim is supported by virtual lesion simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Profiles of neuropsychological impairments in human patients with focal thalamic lesions support the simulated lesion results.
source: This simulation result was further supported by profiles of neuropsychological impairments in human patients with focal thalamic lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by empirical lesion data from human patients.

claim: The application of dimensionality reduction techniques on whole-brain imaging data has revealed a relatively low-dimensional organization of cortical neural activity.
source: The application of dimensionality reduction techniques on whole-brain imaging data has revealed a relatively low-dimensional organization of cortical neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established findings in the field.

claim: The number of variables required to explain a large amount of variance in distributed neural activity is far lower than the total number of variables in the data.
source: Specifically, the number of variables required to explain a large amount of variance in distributed neural activity is far lower than the total number of variables in the data (MacDowell and Buschman, 2020; Nakai and Nishimoto, 2020; Shine et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Low-dimensional organization may reflect an elementary set of information processes implemented by distributed brain systems.
source: This low-dimensional organization may reflect an elementary set of information processes implemented by distributed brain systems (Cunningham and Yu, 2014; Yeo et al., 2016), in which different tasks selectively engaged selective latent activity patterns depending on the specific processing requirements of individual tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents a theoretical interpretation.

claim: Associative regions in frontal and parietal cortices are involved in executing a wide array of tasks.
source: In support of this prediction, studies have found that associative regions in frontal and parietal cortices are involved in executing a wide array of tasks (Cole et al., 2013; Duncan, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Task-flexible regions have diverging connectivity with multiple brain systems and are thought to perform integrative functions.
source: These task-flexible regions, also commonly referred to as brain hubs (Gratton et al., 2018; van den Heuvel and Sporns, 2013), have diverging connectivity with multiple brain systems, and are thought to perform integrative functions that allow perceptual inputs to interact with contextual task representations for adaptive task control (Bertolero et al., 2018; Bertolero et al., 2015; Ito et al., 2022; Nee, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Lesions to hub regions are associated with task impairments across multiple functional domains.
source: The behavioral significance of brain hubs is affirmed by lesion studies demonstrating that lesions to hub regions are associated with task impairments across multiple functional domains (Hwang et al., 2021; Reber et al., 2021; Warren et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to lesion studies.

claim: The human thalamus contains a complete representation of intrinsic cortical functional networks.
source: Our previous studies demonstrated that the human thalamus contains a complete representation of intrinsic cortical functional networks, and additionally, exhibits a hub-like connectivity profile interlinking multiple cortical systems (Hwang et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Every cortical region receives projections from multiple thalamic nuclei.
source: Given that every cortical region receives projections from multiple thalamic nuclei and that the thalamus mediates striatal and cerebellar influences on cortical (Shine, 2020), the thalamocortical system is ideally suited to shape cortex-wide activity patterns that instantiate cognitive representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The thalamus mediates striatal and cerebellar influences on cortical activity.
source: Given that every cortical region receives projections from multiple thalamic nuclei and that the thalamus mediates striatal and cerebellar influences on cortical (Shine, 2020), the thalamocortical system is ideally suited to shape cortex-wide activity patterns that instantiate cognitive representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shine, 2020.

claim: In the MDTB dataset, 21 subjects performed 25 behavioral tasks.
source: In the first dataset, the multi-domain task battery (MDTB) dataset, 21 subjects performed 25 behavioral tasks (King et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: In the N&N dataset, 6 subjects performed 103 tasks.
source: In the second dataset, the Nakai and Nishimoto (N&N) dataset, 6 subjects performed 103 tasks (Nakai and Nishimoto, 2020).
evidence: This claim describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: The top 3 thalamic activity components can explain up to 50% of the variance across tasks for the MDTB dataset.
source: Similar to previous studies that focused on cortical activity patterns (Nakai and Nishimoto, 2020; Shine et al., 2019a), we found that the top 3 thalamic activity components can explain up to 50% of the variance across tasks for the MDTB dataset and 36% for the N&N dataset, in which each task is associated with a weighted sum of these components (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claim: The top 3 thalamic activity components can explain 36% of the variance for the N&N dataset.
source: Similar to previous studies that focused on cortical activity patterns (Nakai and Nishimoto, 2020; Shine et al., 2019a), we found that the top 3 thalamic activity components can explain up to 50% of the variance across tasks for the MDTB dataset and 36% for the N&N dataset, in which each task is associated with a weighted sum of these components (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Up to 57% of variances across task activity patterns in the human thalamus can be explained by 10 components.
source: Repeating the PCA for each subject (without averaging across subjects) revealed similar findings, where up to 57% of variances across task activity patterns in the human thalamus can be explained by 10 components (Figure 1C; 73% for MDTB, 57% for N&N).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-subject PCA analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: For the MDTB dataset, the anterior, medial, medio-posterior, and dorsal thalamus exhibited strong task hub properties.
source: Results showed that for the MDTB dataset, the anterior, medial, medio-posterior, and dorsal thalamus exhibited strong task hub properties (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by task hub analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The spatial correlation between task hub metrics from the two datasets was r=0.36.
source: For the N&N dataset, the posterior thalamus did not exhibit strong task hub property, and the spatial correlation between task hub metrics from the two datasets was r=0.36.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial correlation analysis between datasets.

claim: The task hubs showed significant spatial correspondence with FC hubs.
source: The task hubs showed significant spatial correspondence with FC hubs (Figure 2A; spatial correlation: MDTB mean = 0.17, SD = 0.083, p<0.001; N&N mean = 0.17, SD = 0.05, p<0.001; spatial correlation between MDTB and N&N: r=0.55).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial correlation analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Tasks hubs were most strongly coupled with associate regions in the frontal and parietal cortex.
source: We found that tasks hubs were most strongly coupled with associate regions in the frontal and parietal cortex, for example, the lateral frontal, the insula, the dorsal medial prefrontal, and the intraparietal cortices (Figure 2B; spatial correlation between MDTB and N&N: r=0.46).
evidence: This claim is supported by thalamocortical projection analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The task hub values were highest in the anterior and mediodorsal nuclei in both datasets.
source: In both datasets, we found the task hub values to be highest in the anterior and mediodorsal nuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis using the Morel atlas shown in Figure 3.

claim: The anterior and mediodorsal nuclei have strong reciprocal connectivity with frontal regions.
source: These nuclei groups are known to have strong reciprocal connectivity with frontal regions (Giguere and Goldman-Rakic, 1988; Selemon and Goldman-Rakic, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The mean prediction accuracy of the thalamocortical activity flow model was 0.29 for the MDTB dataset and 0.15 for the N&N dataset.
source: The mean prediction accuracy of the thalamocortical activity flow model was 0.29 for the MDTB dataset and 0.15 for the N&N dataset (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by activity flow model results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: After accounting for the noise ceiling, the normalized prediction accuracy was 0.5 for MDTB and 0.62 for N&N.
source: After accounting for the noise ceiling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the normalized prediction accuracy was 0.5 for MDTB and 0.62 for N&N (Figure 4C), which indicates that the thalamocortical model was able to account for up to 38% of variance in task-evoked activity patterns in the cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by noise-normalized activity flow model results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The thalamocortical activity flow model outperformed the null models for the MDTB dataset.
source: We further found that thalamocortical activity flow model outperformed the null models, except for the N&N dataset when compared to the averaged evoked pattern model (Figure 4C; MDTB thalamocortical model vs. null model: t(20) = 11.22, p<0.001; MDTB thalamocortical model vs. uniformed evoked model: t(20) = 12.05, p<0.001; MDTB thalamocortical model vs. averaged pattern model: t(20) = 6.88, p<0.001; N&N thalamocortical model vs. null model: t(5) = 11.22, p=0.018; N&N thalamocortical model vs. uniformed evoked model: t(5) = 4.75, p=0.005; N&N thalamocortical model vs. averaged pattern model: t(5) = 1.61, p=0.17).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparisons of model performance.

claim: The thalamocortical model outperformed all comparison models including cortical and subcortical regions.
source: However, the thalamocortical model outperformed all comparison models.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of activity flow models across brain regions.

claim: Removing voxels with strong task hub estimates decreased the prediction accuracy in cortical task-evoked activity patterns.
source: For both datasets, we found that removing voxels with strong task hub estimates decreased the prediction accuracy in cortical task-evoked activity patterns (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by virtual lesion simulation results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was a significant negative association between reduction in prediction and percentile rank of task hub metrics removed.
source: We fitted a regression model to test the relationship between reduction in prediction and percentile rank of task hub metrics removed, and found significant negative associations (MDTB activity flow prediction: b=–0.43, SE = 0.019, t=–22.63, p<0.001; N&N activity flow prediction: b=–0.1, SE = 0.028, t=–3.79, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of virtual lesion effects.

claim: Thalamic voxels with the strongest impact on prediction performance were spatially located in the anterior, medial, mediodorsal, and medial posterior thalamus.
source: Furthermore, thalamic voxels with the strongest impact on prediction performance were spatially located in the anterior, medial, mediodorsal, and medial posterior thalamus that we previously identified as task hubs (Figure 5B; spatial correlation between MDTB and N&N r=0.29).
evidence: This claim is supported by virtual lesion analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Twelve patients exhibited impairment across multiple domains (MM group).
source: Twelve out of 20 patients had significant impairment (z<–1.645) reported in more than two functional domains, and thus were classified as the MM patient group.
evidence: This claim is supported by neuropsychological assessment data from patients.

claim: Eight patients had significant impairment in one or fewer domains (SM group).
source: The rest of the 8 patients had significant impairment in one or fewer domains, and classified as the SM group.
evidence: This claim is supported by neuropsychological assessment data from patients.

claim: There were no statistically significant differences in the lesion volumes between the MM and SM patient groups.
source: There were no statistically significant differences in the lesion volumes between these two groups of patients (MM group: mean = 1559 mm3, SD = 1370 mm3; SM group: mean = 1073 mm3, SD = 925 mm3; group difference in lesion size, t(18) = 0.87, p=0.39).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of lesion volumes.

claim: Simulated lesions to voxels that overlapped with lesion sites in the MM patient group showed larger reductions in task activity predictions for the N&N dataset.
source: We found that simulated lesions to voxels that overlapped with lesion sites in the MM patient group showed larger reductions in task activity predictions for the N&N dataset but not the MDTB dataset (Figure 6C; MDTB: Komogorov-Smirnov test D=0.048, p=0.065; N&N: Komogorov-Smirnov test D=0.25, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of virtual lesion effects with patient lesion sites shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The thalamocortical system is ideally suited to shape cortex-wide activity patterns that instantiate cognitive representations.
source: Given that every cortical region receives projections from multiple thalamic nuclei and that the thalamus mediates striatal and cerebellar influences on cortical (Shine, 2020), the thalamocortical system is ideally suited to shape cortex-wide activity patterns that instantiate cognitive representations.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on anatomical connectivity patterns and cited literature.

claim: The thalamus may be at the nexus where specific activity patterns can be selectively down- or up-regulated to meet the specific information processing demands of different tasks.
source: We speculate that the thalamus may be at the nexus where specific activity patterns in the thalamus can be selectively down- or up-regulated to meet the specific information processing demands of different tasks.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated as speculation by the authors.

claim: Functions that may be influenced by the thalamocortical system include selection and gain control, adjustment of inter-regional communication, and modulation of cortical excitability.
source: Functions that may be influenced by the thalamocortical system suggested by previous studies include selection and gain control (Halassa and Kastner, 2017), adjustment of inter-regional communication (Hwang et al., 2020b; Saalmann et al., 2012), and modulation of cortical excitability (Kosciessa et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies have found that thalamic activity correlates with the dimensionality and the strength of cross-system coupling between cortical regions.
source: for instance, previous studies have found that thalamic activity correlates with the dimensionality and the strength of cross-system coupling between cortical regions (Garrett et al., 2018; Shine et al., 2019b), and thalamic lesions disrupt the low-dimensional cortical network organization (Hwang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Thalamic lesions disrupt the low-dimensional cortical network organization.
source: for instance, previous studies have found that thalamic activity correlates with the dimensionality and the strength of cross-system coupling between cortical regions (Garrett et al., 2018; Shine et al., 2019b), and thalamic lesions disrupt the low-dimensional cortical network organization (Hwang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The thalamus consists of two classes of thalamocortical projection cells: 'matrix' and 'core' cells.
source: For instance, the thalamus consists of two classes of thalamocortical projection cells, 'matrix' and 'core' cells, where core cells target specific granular cortical structures, and matrix cells diffusely project to multiple brain regions (Jones, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Core cells target specific granular cortical structures, and matrix cells diffusely project to multiple brain regions.
source: For instance, the thalamus consists of two classes of thalamocortical projection cells, 'matrix' and 'core' cells, where core cells target specific granular cortical structures, and matrix cells diffusely project to multiple brain regions (Jones, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The thalamus is modulated by inputs from other subcortical structures, such as the reticular nucleus, the basal ganglia, the superior colliculus, and the cerebellum.
source: Furthermore, the thalamus is modulated by inputs from other subcortical structures, such as the reticular nucleus, the basal ganglia, the superior colliculus, and the cerebellum (Bostan and Strick, 2018; Hwang et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Network hubs in the frontal and parietal cortices broadly participate in cognitive tasks across different functional domains.
source: Network hubs in the frontal and parietal cortices have also been found to broadly participate in cognitive tasks across different functional domains (Bertolero et al., 2015; Yeo et al., 2016), likely reflect its role in instantiating task representations (Schumacher and Hazeltine, 2016) and support cross-domain cognitive functions that arise from brain-wide network interactions (Gratton et al., 2018; van den Heuvel and Sporns, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Thalamic task hubs were most strongly coupled with multiple regions across frontal and parietal associative cortices.
source: We found that thalamic task hubs were most strongly coupled with multiple regions across frontal and parietal associative cortices, including subregions that found to exhibit functional specialization for specific tasks as well as task-flexible regions (Yeo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by thalamocortical coupling analysis.

claim: Selective regions within the frontal and parietal cortices have been hypothesized to be part of a flexible multiple-demand system.
source: Several selective regions within the frontal and parietal cortices have been hypothesized to be part of a flexible multiple-demand system (Assem et al., 2020) and thus, these thalamic subregions may be part of a core system whose functions are required to perform specific computations that are common across many different task contexts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and includes an inference about thalamic subregions.

claim: In rodent models, the medial thalamus excites task-relevant and inhibits task-irrelevant cortical activity that encodes working memory representations.
source: One hypothesis, suggested by findings from rodent models, is that the medial thalamus excites task-relevant and inhibits task-irrelevant cortical activity that encodes working memory representations (Mukherjee et al., 2021; Rikhye et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to rodent studies.

claim: In human subjects, thalamocortical interactions between thalamic task hubs and frontoparietal systems may control task representations that bind sensory, motor, and contextual information.
source: Thus, in human subjects, thalamocortical interactions between thalamic task hubs and frontoparietal systems may control task representations that bind sensory, motor, and contextual information that are necessary for adaptive behavior across tasks (Schumacher and Hazeltine, 2016).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from rodent findings and citation.

claim: The thalamocortical activity flow model cannot establish the directionality of thalamic activity influencing cortical activity.
source: On important limitation of our study is that our thalamocortical activity flow model cannot establish the directionality of thalamic activity influencing cortical activity.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Brain systems instantiate cognitive representations via recurrent connectivity among cortical regions and the thalamus, as well as integrating inputs from other brain structures.
source: It is more likely that brain systems instantiate cognitive representations via recurrent connectivity among cortical regions and the thalamus, as well as integrating inputs from other brain structures.
evidence: This claim represents an inference about brain system organization.

claim: Including all brain regions into the activity flow model can substantially improve model performance in predicting task-specific activity patterns.
source: As discussed above, including all brain regions into the activity flow model can substantially improve model performance in predicting task-specific activity patterns (Cole et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The posterior thalamus exhibited strong task hub property in the MDTB dataset but not the N&N dataset.
source: Another important limitation is that the posterior thalamus exhibited strong task hub property in the MDTB dataset but not the N&N dataset.
evidence: This is a discrepancy observed in the data between the two datasets.

claim: The discrepancy in posterior thalamus task hub property could be related to differences in behavioral tasks across the two datasets.
source: We suspect this could be related to differences in behavioral tasks across the two datasets, and speculatively, to the increased noise in the N&N dataset, given the lower number of observations per task and lower subcortical signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the cause of the discrepancy.

claim: Three out of the original 24 subjects in the MDTB dataset were excluded because they did not have all tasks available after removing high noise datapoints.
source: The MDTB dataset included fMRI data from 21 subjects (13 women, 8 men; mean age = 23.28 years, SD = 2.13; we excluded 3 out of the original 24 subjects that did not have all tasks available after removing high noise datapoints).
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria applied in the study.

claim: Both datasets were preprocessed using fMRIPrep version 20.1.1.
source: Both datasets were preprocessed using fMRIPrep version 20.1.1 (Esteban et al., 2019) to reduce noise and transform data from subject native space to the ICBM 152 Nonlinear Asymmetrical template version 2009c for group analysis (Fonov et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the preprocessing methods used in the study.

claim: No spatial smoothing was performed on the fMRI data.
source: We did not perform any spatial smoothing.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in data preprocessing.

claim: High motion volumes with framewise displacement >0.2 mm were removed from data analyses via the censoring option.
source: High motion volumes (framewise displacement >0.2 mm) were removed from data analyses via the censoring option, and subjects with tasks with more than 40% of the data censored were dropped from further analyses (three MDTB subjects dropped).
evidence: This describes the motion correction procedure used in the study.

claim: Subjects with tasks with more than 40% of the data censored were dropped from further analyses.
source: High motion volumes (framewise displacement >0.2 mm) were removed from data analyses via the censoring option, and subjects with tasks with more than 40% of the data censored were dropped from further analyses (three MDTB subjects dropped).
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria based on motion.

claim: Residuals from the GLM were used for subsequent FC analysis to minimize the potential confound of averaged evoked responses inflating estimates of FC.
source: Critically, we used residuals from the GLM instead of the preprocessed functional timeseries to minimize the potential confound of averaged evoked responses inflating estimates of FC (Cole et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice to reduce confounds in FC estimation.

claim: The correlations between task regressors and thalamus/cortical timeseries used for calculating FC were weak, suggesting that task-evoked activations likely did not bias the activity flow analysis.
source: We found the correlations to be weak (with cortical ROI timeseries, mean r=−2.02 * 10–10, SD = 1.06* 10–8; with thalamic voxel timeseries, mean r=4.37 * 10–10, SD = 1.27* 10–10). These weak correlations suggest that task-evoked activations likely did not bias our activity flow analysis.
evidence: This is a validation check showing that task-evoked activity was successfully removed from FC estimates.

claim: Patients were selected from the Iowa Neurological Patient Registry and had focal lesions caused by ischemic or hemorrhagic strokes restricted to the thalamus.
source: Briefly, these patients were selected from the Iowa Neurological Patient Registry, and had focal lesions caused by ischemic or hemorrhagic strokes restricted to the thalamus (age = 18–70 years, mean = 55.8 years, SD = 13.94 years, 13 males).
evidence: This describes the patient selection criteria for the lesion study.

claim: All participants gave written informed consent, and the study was approved by the University of Iowa Institutional Review Board.
source: All participants gave written informed consent, and the study was approved by the University of Iowa Institutional Review Board (IRB protocol #200105018).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval and consent procedures.

claim: Behavioral deficits were assessed using a set of standardized neuropsychological tests including TMT Part B, BNT, COWA, RAVLT, Rey Complex Figure tests, and others.
source: Behavioral deficits were assessed using a set of standardized neuropsychological tests: (1) executive function using the Trail Making Test Part B (TMT Part B); (2) verbal naming using the Boston Naming Test (BNT); (3) verbal fluency using the Controlled Oral Word Association Test (COWA); (4) immediate learning using the first trial test score from the Rey Auditory-Verbal Learning Test (RAVLT); (5) total learning by summing scores from RAVLT, trials 1 through 5; (6) long-term memory recall using the RAVLT 30 min delayed recall score; (7) long-term memory recognition using the RAVLT 30 min delayed recognition score; (8) visuospatial memory using the Rey Complex Figure delayed recall score; (9) psychomotor function using the Trail Making Test Part A (TMT Part A); and (10) construction using the Rey Complex Figure copy test.
evidence: This describes the neuropsychological assessment battery used in the patient study.

claim: All test scores were converted to age-adjusted z-scores using the mean and standard deviation from published population normative data.
source: To account for age-related effects, all test scores were converted to age-adjusted z-scores using the mean and standard deviation from published population normative data.
evidence: This describes the normalization procedure for neuropsychological test scores.

claim: Significant impairment was defined as z<–1.645.
source: Twelve out of 20 patients had significant impairment (z<–1.645) reported in more than two functional domains, and thus were classified as the MM patient group.
evidence: This defines the threshold for determining significant impairment.

claim: The thalamus is not a homogenous structure and can be divided into different subdivisions or nuclei based on its functional and histological properties.
source: Given that the thalamus is not a homogenous structure and can be divided into different subdivisions or nuclei based on its functional and histological properties, we summarized the spatial distribution of task hub estimates (CompW) using two different thalamic atlases (Figure 3).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about thalamic organization.

claim: The Morel atlas maps human thalamic nuclei based on cyto- and myelo-architecture information in stained slices from five postmortem human brains.
source: First, the Morel atlas was used to determine the location of different thalamic nuclei Krauth et al., 2010; this atlas maps human thalamic nuclei based on cyto- and myelo-architecture information in stained slices from five postmortem human brains, and further transformed to the template space.
evidence: This describes the Morel atlas used in the study.

claim: Each thalamic voxel was assigned to one of the seven canonical cortical function networks for the network atlas.
source: Second, for the network atlas, we assigned each thalamic voxel to one of the seven canonical cortical function networks (Schaefer et al., 2018) that we used for calculating network hubs.
evidence: This describes the network parcellation approach used in the study.

claim: Thalamic task hubs do not overlap with one functional network parcellation or thalamic nucleus, instead overlap with multiple thalamic parcellations and nuclei.
source: Overall, these results suggest that thalamic task hubs do not overlap with one functional network parcellation or thalamic nucleus, instead overlap with multiple thalamic parcellations and nuclei.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the atlas-based analysis results.

claim: The medial pulvinar showed high task hub value in the MDTB dataset but not in the N&N dataset.
source: We also found the medial pulvinar to show high task hub value but only in the MDTB dataset, likely because the N&N dataset did not show high task hub value in the posterior thalamus.
evidence: This is a dataset-specific finding from the atlas-based analysis.

claim: In the MDTB dataset, the DF parcellation (which overlapped with the anterior medial, medial, and posterior medial thalamus) showed the highest task hub value.
source: For example, in the MDTB dataset, the DF parcellation (which overlapped with the anterior medial, medial, and posterior medial thalamus) was found to show the highest task hub value.
evidence: This is a finding from the network atlas analysis.

claim: In the N&N dataset, the FP parcellation, which covered the dorsal bank of the medial thalamus, showed the highest task hub value.
source: For the N&N dataset, the posterior thalamus did not exhibit high task hub value, but the FP parcellation, which covered the dorsal bank of the medial thalamus, showed the highest task hub value.
evidence: This is a finding from the network atlas analysis.

claim: Lateral ROIs in the visual network showed the highest normalized prediction accuracy among cortical comparison models.
source: For example for both datasets, lateral ROIs in the visual network showed the highest normalized prediction accuracy, but still statistically weaker than the thalamocortical activity flow model (MDTB: t(20) = 2.91, p=0.008; N&N: t(5) = 3.3, p=0.021).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of activity flow models across brain regions.

claim: The thalamocortical model was able to account for up to 38% of variance in task-evoked activity patterns in the cortex.
source: After accounting for the noise ceiling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the normalized prediction accuracy was 0.5 for MDTB and 0.62 for N&N (Figure 4C), which indicates that the thalamocortical model was able to account for up to 38% of variance in task-evoked activity patterns in the cortex.
evidence: This is calculated from the normalized prediction accuracy values.
